about: The driver's behaviour, as data rather than as prose.
A specification nobody can run is a specification every implementation reads
differently. So this file is what 'the Python binding is correct' means, and
the Rust driver runs exactly the same file - which is what stops the reference
implementation and the specification drifting apart, because there is only one
of them.
A runner is about forty lines in any language: open a scratch database, run
each case's setup, run each step, compare. drivers/README.md walks through it.
VALUES are one-key objects so that NULL and the empty string can never be
confused, which is the same reason the driver has a Null variant:
{"null": true}   {"int": 7}   {"real": 0.5}
A blob is a byte array rather than base64 so that no runner needs a decoder.
A CASE may set "connection": "per_call", which asks the runner to open a fresh
connection for every setup statement and every step, all continuing one session.
That is the shape a driver in another language is forced into - a connection that
borrows its database cannot be held by a garbage-collected caller, and a C handle
cannot hold a borrow at all - and it is what the C ABI does on every call. A runner
whose connections already work that way satisfies it by doing nothing. Absent means
one connection for the whole case, which is every other case here.
A STEP asserts whatever keys it carries and ignores the rest, so a case can
check a row count without pinning the rows, or a status without pinning the
message. The keys are:
sql               the statement (required)
params            values bound to ?1, ?2, ...
limit             rows to hand back; absent means all
columns           the result column names, in order
rows              every row handed back, in order
affected          rows changed; use null to assert it is a query
total             rows produced before the limit - exact, not an estimate
more              whether the limit cut anything off
status            the failure's status name; absent means it must succeed
message_contains  a substring of the failure's message
feature_contains  a substring of the construct named by an unsupported refusal
VERSION 2 (task-2036) adds the fts, hybrid, transaction_failure, values, status and
identifiers groups, and with them the two fields that say who can run what.
A case may declare NEEDS, a list of capabilities out of `capabilities` above. A
runner that does not have one skips those cases and says so in `skipped_by`,
naming what it lacks and why. `tooling::every_binding_runs_the_whole_suite` reads
both: a runner has to run every case whose needs it satisfies, and a runner that
ran fewer has to have said in this file which capability it is missing.
The three command line wrappers - npm, Go and PHP - lack `session`, and the
reason is the shape rather than an omission: each call is a process, so a
transaction, a savepoint or a temporary table cannot outlive one step. Rows do,
because they are in the file. Bytes do too: the command line binds a blob as
{"blob":"<hex>"} and renders one back as the text x'<hex>', so a process
runner carries them once it knows that rendering.
Each runner writes _agent_output/conformance/<language>.json naming the cases it
ran, which is what the guard reads.

cases.name: insert_then_select
cases.about: The shape everything else rests on: a write reports what it changed, and a read gives it back.
setup: CREATE TABLE t (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT a, b FROM t ORDER BY a

cases.name: every_value_kind_round_trips
cases.about: All five kinds, including the two that are easy to get wrong: a blob holding a NUL byte, and text that is not ASCII. A driver that renders values as text loses the first; one that uses C strings truncates it.
setup: CREATE TABLE v (k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value BLOB)

steps.sql: SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'null'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'int'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'real'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'text'
SELECT value FROM v WHERE k = 'blob'

cases.name: null_is_not_the_empty_string
cases.about: The fault a grid drawing both as nothing would hide: a column never filled in and one filled in with nothing are not the same fact about a row.
setup: CREATE TABLE n (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT b FROM n WHERE a = 1
SELECT b FROM n WHERE a = 2

cases.name: a_limit_cuts_the_rows_handed_back_and_total_stays_exact
cases.about: The engine materialises, so `total` was counted rather than estimated. That is what lets a grid say `1-2 of 5` and mean it.
setup: CREATE TABLE many (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (1)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (2)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (3)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (4)
INSERT INTO many VALUES (5)

steps.sql: SELECT a FROM many ORDER BY a
SELECT a FROM many ORDER BY a

cases.name: parameters_are_bound_not_pasted
cases.about: A value that would be syntax if it were pasted into the statement.
setup: CREATE TABLE p (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT b FROM p WHERE a = ?1

cases.name: a_missing_table_is_not_found_and_a_typo_is_syntax
cases.about: The three refusals a caller has to be able to tell apart. This case and the next are the whole point of the driver.
setup: CREATE TABLE people (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: an_unimplemented_construct_refuses_by_name
cases.about: A construct the engine has not built reports `unsupported` and names itself, which is a different thing from a statement that is wrong. A binding that folds this into its general error type has thrown the design away. The example moves as the engine grows: it was VACUUM before that was built, a second ON CONFLICT clause before that was built, and is now an encryption key on ATTACH. When that is built, repoint this at whatever still is rather than deleting the case.
setup: CREATE TABLE conflicts (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT UNIQUE)

cases.name: a_constraint_refuses_a_write
cases.about: A refusal that is the schema doing its job, and must not read as either a syntax error or a missing feature.
setup: CREATE TABLE u (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT UNIQUE)
INSERT INTO u VALUES (1, 'one')

cases.name: a_transaction_commits_all_of_it
setup: CREATE TABLE c (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: a_rollback_undoes_all_of_it
cases.about: Including the row written before the one that failed, which is the half a driver that stopped at the first error but did not roll back would leave behind.
setup: CREATE TABLE r (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO r VALUES (1)

cases.name: a_savepoint_rolls_back_to_itself
setup: CREATE TABLE s (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: a_delete_that_matched_nothing_says_zero_rather_than_failing
cases.about: Zero changed rows is an answer, not an error. A row editor's rule that every statement must change exactly one row is built on being told the difference.
setup: CREATE TABLE d (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)
INSERT INTO d VALUES (1)

cases.name: returning_gives_rows_and_a_count
cases.about: The one statement that fills both, which is why `affected` is decided by the count rather than by whether there were columns.
setup: CREATE TABLE ret (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: INSERT INTO ret VALUES (1, 'one') RETURNING a, b

cases.name: the_schema_can_be_read_back
cases.about: `sqlite_schema` is a readable table and it holds the CREATE statement as it was typed, which is what lets a consumer show a person what they wrote rather than something composed from a catalogue.
setup: CREATE TABLE shown (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT type, name FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name = 'shown'
SELECT sql FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name = 'shown'

rows.text: CREATE TABLE shown (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

cases.name: reserved_word_column_names
cases.about: `left` and `right` are ordinary column names in SQLite - a diff table, a tree, a stereo channel, a page layout - and its name production accepts the join keywords and `INDEXED` directly rather than through the fallback set. A database using them imported as `corrupt` until that was fixed, so this case pins every position a name can appear in: the declaration, a bare reference, a qualified one, an ORDER BY, and an explicit alias. The last step is the other half of the rule: a bare alias written with no AS takes the narrow fallback set, so `SELECT left right FROM pairs` is a syntax error in SQLite and has to stay one here - that is what keeps `FROM t LEFT JOIN u` a join rather than a table aliased `left`.
setup: CREATE TABLE pairs (left TEXT, right TEXT, inner TEXT, outer TEXT, cross TEXT, indexed TEXT)
INSERT INTO pairs VALUES ('a', 'b', 'i', 'o', 'c', 'x')
INSERT INTO pairs VALUES ('c', 'd', 'i', 'o', 'c', 'x')

steps.sql: SELECT left, right FROM pairs ORDER BY left
SELECT pairs.inner, pairs.outer, pairs.cross, pairs.indexed FROM pairs WHERE left = 'a'
SELECT left AS right, right AS left FROM pairs WHERE left = 'a'
SELECT sql FROM sqlite_schema WHERE name = 'pairs'

rows.text: CREATE TABLE pairs (left TEXT, right TEXT, inner TEXT, outer TEXT, cross TEXT, indexed TEXT)

cases.name: a_temp_table_survives_a_connection_per_call
cases.about: A temporary table belongs to a session, and a caller that hands out a connection per call has to stay in one or it loses everything a session scopes. This case runs every statement on its own connection, so it passes only if the driver can continue a session: the Rust driver used to expose connect() and not connect_as(), and the C ABI opened a new session on every call - so a CREATE TEMP TABLE typed into a query console was gone by the next statement, an ATTACH did not outlive its own call, and a connection pragma had to be re-applied every time. The last two steps are the rest of the scope: an ordinary table is visible either way, and a temp table shadows a permanent one of the same name, which is only observable if the temp one is still there.
setup: CREATE TABLE kept (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)
INSERT INTO kept VALUES (1, 'permanent')

steps.sql: CREATE TEMP TABLE scratch (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)
SELECT a, b FROM scratch ORDER BY a
CREATE TEMP TABLE kept (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)

cases.name: a_columns_declared_type_is_reported_and_an_expression_has_none
cases.about: An expression genuinely has no declared type, and the empty string is the honest answer rather than a guess taken from the first row - which would be a different answer on a different page of the same query.
setup: CREATE TABLE typed (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT)
INSERT INTO typed VALUES (1, 'one')

cases.name: a_vector_column_binds_and_reads_back_as_a_blob
cases.about: A VECTOR(N) column is N little-endian f32s and the driver carries it as a blob, so a binding that renders values as text or that uses C strings loses it: the first float of [1,0,0] is 0x0000803f and its first byte is a NUL. No case here named a vector before, so nothing proved that one bound as a parameter or read back as a blob survives the driver, the C ABI or any binding.
setup: CREATE TABLE point (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, at VECTOR(3))

steps.sql: SELECT at FROM point WHERE id = 1
SELECT vector_dims(at) FROM point ORDER BY id

cases.name: fts5_matches_and_ranks
cases.about: An FTS5 index answers a term, a phrase and a prefix, ranks by bm25(), and forgets a document that was deleted. Nothing in this file named FTS5 before, so a binding could ship unable to reach the half of this engine that is not ordinary SQL.
setup: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE docs USING fts5(title, body)
INSERT INTO docs(rowid, title, body) VALUES (1, 'alpha note', 'the quick brown fox jumps')
INSERT INTO docs(rowid, title, body) VALUES (2, 'beta note', 'the lazy brown dog sleeps')
INSERT INTO docs(rowid, title, body) VALUES (3, 'gamma note', 'quick foxes and lazy dogs')

steps.sql: SELECT rowid FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH 'brown' ORDER BY rowid
SELECT rowid FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH '"brown fox"' ORDER BY rowid
SELECT rowid FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH 'fox*' ORDER BY rowid
SELECT rowid FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH 'lazy' ORDER BY bm25(docs), rowid

cases.name: fts5_forgets_a_deleted_document
cases.about: A delete has to reach the index as well as the content table. An index that kept the doclist would answer a MATCH with a rowid that is not there, which a caller reads as a row it can fetch.
setup: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE docs USING fts5(title, body)
INSERT INTO docs(rowid, title, body) VALUES (1, 'alpha', 'the quick brown fox')
INSERT INTO docs(rowid, title, body) VALUES (2, 'beta', 'the lazy brown dog')

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH 'brown'
SELECT rowid FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH 'brown' ORDER BY rowid

cases.name: hybrid_search_answers_and_ranks
cases.about: `inillucent_search` is this engine's own hybrid index and the reason a caller would choose it over SQLite. A binding that cannot reach it can carry an application's rows and not its retrieval.
setup: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE hy USING inillucent_search(title, body)
INSERT INTO hy(rowid, title, body) VALUES (1, 'alpha', 'ledger pages and trees')
INSERT INTO hy(rowid, title, body) VALUES (2, 'beta', 'ledger commits and segments')
INSERT INTO hy(rowid, title, body) VALUES (3, 'gamma', 'nothing in common here')

steps.sql: SELECT rowid FROM hy('ledger', 5) ORDER BY rank

cases.name: a_multi_row_insert_that_collides_keeps_nothing
cases.about: Four rows in one INSERT, colliding on the third. A statement is atomic whether or not it is inside a transaction, so the answer is zero rows either way - and a binding that reported the affected count of the rows that went in before the collision would be telling a caller two rows were written.
setup: CREATE TABLE u (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

cases.name: the_same_collision_inside_a_transaction_keeps_nothing
cases.about: The same statement inside an explicit transaction that is then committed. The failed statement leaves nothing and the transaction is still usable, which is the property an application relies on when it retries.
setup: CREATE TABLE u (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY)

steps.sql: SELECT a FROM u ORDER BY a

cases.name: a_forty_kilobyte_value_round_trips
cases.about: Larger than a 32,768 byte page and ten times larger than a 4,096 byte one, so the value crosses the extent threshold at every page size the engine builds at. A binding with a fixed buffer somewhere truncates here and nowhere else.
setup: CREATE TABLE big (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)

cases.name: the_empty_and_the_absent_are_three_different_values
cases.about: An empty string, an empty blob and a NULL are three values, and a layer that renders them the same has already lost the difference.
setup: CREATE TABLE e (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, t TEXT, b BLOB, n)

steps.sql: INSERT INTO e VALUES (1, '', x'', NULL)
SELECT typeof(t), typeof(b), typeof(n) FROM e
SELECT count(*) FROM e WHERE t = ''
SELECT count(*) FROM e WHERE n IS NULL

cases.name: integers_at_the_edges_of_i64
cases.about: The smallest integer, the largest, and the odd one above 2^53 that a double cannot hold. A binding that carried values through a language's own number type loses the last of these silently, which is how an identifier becomes a different identifier. The last step records something worth knowing: an integer overflow at run time is reported with the status `syntax`, which is the status a caller reads as `reword your SQL`. Asserted as what it is rather than as what it should be, which is rule 1.3.
setup: CREATE TABLE n (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v)

steps.sql: SELECT v, typeof(v) FROM n ORDER BY id

cases.name: a_negative_zero_and_a_value_that_is_not_a_number
cases.about: `-0.0` is a real that equals zero, and `0.0/0.0` is NULL rather than a float nothing can compare - which is SQLite's rule and is what a binding has to carry rather than its language's own NaN.
setup: CREATE TABLE f (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v)

steps.sql: SELECT typeof(v), v = 0.0 FROM f WHERE id = 1
SELECT typeof(v) FROM f WHERE id = 2

cases.name: a_nul_byte_inside_text_is_stored_and_shortens_length
cases.about: `length()` counts to the NUL and the stored bytes go past it, which is what a binding that hands values to C as NUL-terminated strings gets wrong - it would read `a` where the row holds three bytes. Asserted as the hex, because that is the only rendering that carries the byte after the NUL.
setup: CREATE TABLE z (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, t TEXT)

cases.name: composed_and_decomposed_text_stay_two_values
cases.about: The same word in NFC and in NFD is two different strings and has to stay two. A binding that normalised on the way in or out would make two rows one, and nothing would say so.
setup: CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, v TEXT)

steps.sql: SELECT id, hex(v), length(v) FROM t ORDER BY id
SELECT count(*) FROM t WHERE v = char(99,97,102,233)

cases.name: identifiers_that_need_quoting
cases.about: A table name with an accent and a space, a column called `select`, and a column name with a space in it. A binding that builds SQL by concatenation rather than quoting fails here and reads correctly everywhere else.
setup: CREATE TABLE "ordér 1" ("a column" INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, "select" TEXT)
INSERT INTO "ordér 1" VALUES (1, 'x')

steps.sql: SELECT count(*) FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = 'ordér 1'

cases.name: every_status_a_caller_branches_on
cases.about: Four refusals in one case, each asserting the status name rather than the message. A binding that folds them into one error type has thrown away the thing this driver has that a string does not.
setup: CREATE TABLE s (a INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, b TEXT UNIQUE)
INSERT INTO s VALUES (1, 'one')

steps.sql: SELECT a FROM s WHERE (a, b) IN (SELECT a, b FROM s)

cases.name: bytes_read_back_are_bytes
cases.about: Bytes go in and the same bytes come back, proven by binding what came back into a second statement rather than by comparing it with itself. task-2066 section 4.1.15: `--output json` rendered a blob as the string "x'00ff'" typed `text`, so Node, Go, PHP and the subprocess half of Python could write bytes and not read them. The existing round-trip case did not catch it because both sides of its comparison came back as the same wrong string.
setup: CREATE TABLE bytes_back (k TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value BLOB)

steps.sql: SELECT value FROM bytes_back WHERE k = 'first'
SELECT typeof(value) FROM bytes_back WHERE k = 'first'
SELECT length(value) FROM bytes_back WHERE k = 'first'
SELECT hex(value) FROM bytes_back WHERE k = 'first'
SELECT count(*) FROM bytes_back a JOIN bytes_back b ON a.value = b.value WHERE a.k = 'first' AND b.k = 'second'

groups.core: the shape everything else rests on: a write reports what it changed, a read gives it back, a parameter binds
groups.values: values at their edges - the empty, the absent, the enormous, the ones a language's own number type loses
groups.status: the failure statuses a caller branches on, asserted by name
groups.transaction_failure: a statement that fails part way, inside a transaction and outside one
groups.identifiers: names that need quoting, and a table wide enough to find a fixed array
groups.fts: the FTS5 index: a term, a phrase, a prefix, a ranking, and a delete the index has to hear about
groups.hybrid: `inillucent_search`, which is the reason a caller would choose this engine over SQLite

capabilities.session: the runner can hold one connection across a case's steps, so a transaction, a savepoint or a temporary table survives from one step to the next

npm.why: the npm package wraps the command line: every call is a process, so a transaction, a savepoint or a temporary table cannot outlive one step. Rows do outlive it - they are in the file - so only the five cases that hold one of those are skipped. Held-transaction and two-connection behaviour is graded by crates/inillucent-compat/tests/process_concurrency.rs and busy_timeout.rs, over real processes, which is stronger than a runner could be.

go.why: the same: packages/go wraps the command line, one process per call.

php.why: the same: packages/php wraps the command line, one process per call.

python.why: the Python binding links the C ABI and holds a connection.
